concept.name: Basis risk
concept.definition: The risk that a hedge and the underlying exposure do not move in lockstep — that the basis (spot price of the hedged asset minus the futures or hedge price) changes unexpectedly — leaving residual profit or loss despite hedging.
concept.intuition: Your umbrella covers most of you but not exactly: basis risk is the part of the weather that still gets you wet.
concept.mechanics: Basis b = S - F varies with quality or grade differences, timing mismatches between hedge expiry and the exposure's date, and location or transportation differentials. Hedgers manage it by choosing contracts with the closest grade, location, and timing, or with tailored OTC derivatives, accepting that exchange-traded hedges rarely converge perfectly.
concept.formula: Basis = spot price of hedged asset - futures price of hedge contract; basis risk is the variability of the basis over the hedge horizon.
concept.failure_modes: The basis can blow out precisely in crises, when hedges are most relied upon (cash-futures dislocations in stressed markets); cross-hedges over a different grade or underlying carry structural basis that can trend against the hedger for long periods.
concept.misconceptions: A hedge does not eliminate price risk — it converts it into (usually smaller) basis risk — and at expiry spot and futures converge only for the deliverable grade, not necessarily for the hedger's actual asset.
concept.example: A wheat producer hedges with exchange futures of a different grade and delivery point; if local cash prices fall 40 cents while futures fall only 30, the 10-cent basis widening is an unhedged loss.
